unmapped_findings: Product of strength and ductility of the 1200 °C, 1 h specimen: 3 GPa% (Table 1); this is the lowest among the annealed specimens (700–1200 °C), for which the maximum was 31 GPa% at 900 °C.

The 1200 °C annealed specimen has the largest grains: α₂ (banded ferrite) = 68.4 μm and γ = 36.0 μm (Fig. 9); grain growth, rather than phase-fraction change, is the main reason for the decrease of strength and elongation above 900 °C.
The austenite (γ) volume fraction of the 1200 °C specimen is about 57%, within the narrow 57–63% range that γ occupies between 900 °C and 1200 °C (Fig. 14).
No matrix κ-carbide is detected by XRD in the 1200 °C specimen, but boundary κ-carbide (formed during quenching) exists in the specimen, as it does in all specimens annealed at or above 900 °C.
Yield phenomenon (associated with ferrite steels) only appears in the 700 °C specimen; the 1200 °C annealed specimen shows continuous yielding.

In the 1200 °C specimen the needle-like or plate-like FCC particles in some large α grains will undoubtedly promote cracking, and the ductile fracture area lessens with increasing annealing temperature up to 1200 °C.

The present steel's tensile property comparison (Table 2) lists the (900 °C) present-steel values [UTS 855 MPa, YS 651 MPa, γ+α(40%)+boundary κ, elongation 36.6%, product 31 GPa%] against literature Fe–Mn–Al–C steels; these are the optimum present-steel values, not the 1200 °C values.
